challenge: Parpola's 1994 book was not available with clear rights (lending-only copy), so identifications come from his 1997, 2005, 2008, 2009 and 2010 papers. Parpola names signs by their pictures and the project has no crosswalk from his sign numbers to ICIT codes. The spear and the kaḷam sign could not be coded. The frequency proxy of the base-rate study counts every Sangam token with the same initial letter for one-syllable words (ā, kā). 38 templates leave a wide interval on the ratio.
outcome: On 38 blind adjacent sign pairs (16 identified signs, pairs recurring in at least two distinct texts, published and already-examined pairs removed), Parpola's words form an attested two-member Tamil Lexicon compound for 9 pairs (23.7%) against 4.97 expected for matched random words (13.1%): ratio 1.81, 95% bootstrap interval 0.93-2.72, leave-one-out 1.64-1.98. P1 passes its frozen rule (ratio below 2; kill at 3 with lower bound above 1.5 not reached); 6.7% of random keys reach nine hits. Sensitivities give 1.56-2.42. Most hits pair his word with an unrelated homophone (veḷ-ḷ-āṉai 'white elephant' for āṉ 'cow'); iru-kaṇ 'two eyes' is the one apt reading. The hidden-member template (W1-X / X-W2) holds for 22 of 24 gapped pairs against 82% for random words (ratio 1.11). Parpola's twelve published pairs succeed seven times against 1.15 expected (ratio 6.1, 2.8-11.7). Post-outcome: published pairs succeed at 58% against 24% for blind pairs (one-sided Fisher p = 0.032); at the blind rate, seven successes become likely after about 28 tried pairs.
question: On Indus sign pairs that Parpola never published, frozen with his picture identifications before any Tamil compound is looked up, do his word assignments form attested Tamil Lexicon compounds more often than random words matched on compounding productivity and Sangam frequency (C-0014, P1)?
remedy: Acquired four papers with logged requests and hashes; five subagents extracted identifications under a no-dictionary instruction, with forms checked against page images. Fixed ICIT codes from the 45 objects Parpola cites by CISI number and the 'bull's head' from its printed glyph (ICIT 740). Created a new split through bench.shots, counted pairs on the discovery half, froze protocol, predictions and 15 artifacts before the single confirmation read, and hashed the template list before scoring. A synthetic selftest checked planted compounds, sandhi, both search directions, exact against Monte Carlo rates and the cached search against the base-rate picture_hits. An independent reimplementation reproduced all hits and the ratio (1.79 against 1.81) and differed on one pool boundary word because of segmentation of six rare-diacritic headwords.
retry_when: Parpola's full 1994 identifications (book purchase or loan), a second Tamil dictionary with compounds, or a control language for the same pictures (Sanskrit words scored against Monier-Williams compounds, proposed as C-0014 P4). Rerunning these 38 templates on the same identifications and dictionary adds nothing.
theme: Parpola's Dravidian word assignments scored on Indus sign pairs he did not choose, against matched random Tamil words
title: On Indus sign pairs that Parpola never published, frozen with his picture identifications before any Tamil compound is looked up, do his word assignments form attested Tamil Lexicon compounds more often than random words matched on compounding productivity and Sangam frequency (C-0014, P1)?

authors.agent: session started from the session that wrote C-0014

challenge: Winslow prints compounds without hyphens or romanisation, nested under their root, so members had to be recovered from the nesting and Tamil sandhi. Winslow lists every syllabic letter, ending and particle as a headword. The DSAL text writes every initial e as ஏ. DSAL marks long entries with placeholder pages, which stopped the first download stream early. The frozen design matches replacement words to the anchor word's productivity, which is zero for muruku in Winslow.
outcome: P2 failed under its frozen rule. Winslow has no two-member compound beginning with muruku (the Tamil Lexicon has 7) and 29 with mīṉ as last member (82), so replacement words matched on muruku's productivity have no compounds and none of 2,500 pairs shares a member (rate 0.0, Wilson 95% upper bound 0.15%; threshold above 0.20). Neither Muruka-vēḷ nor veṇ-mīṉ is a Winslow entry, so the veḷ interlock does not exist there; Skanda's name on vēḷ is cevvēḷ. Two of Parpola's five interlocks hold (vaṭa-mīṉ, aṟu-mīṉ) and random words reproduce both in 3.9% of 10,000 draws. Post-outcome: with pools matched to 7 first-member and 29 second-member compounds, random pairs share a member in 14.0% of cases in Winslow and 16.6% in the Lexicon; a complete parse would give muruku two first-member compounds (murukkam-pū, murukkañ-cettal), and pools matched to one compound give 2.8%.
question: Does the veḷ interlock search of REBUS-BASE-RATE-2026-10-21, rerun in Winslow's Tamil-English dictionary of 1862, again find a shared compound member for more than 20% of random replacement pairs, as prediction P2 of C-0014 states?

theme: Chance rate of Parpola's veḷ compound interlock in a second Tamil dictionary (Winslow 1862)

challenge: The fish signs have been examined repeatedly, so only seals absent from the pinned corpus can confirm. Two OCR scans with different errors had to be aligned clause by clause; the personal-name index could not be used. Closure and the Brahmi profile do not separate birth-star names from an ordinary closed sign family with the same profile.
outcome: Calibration: of 757 personal donor occurrences in Lüders's list, 42 (5.5%) carry strictly marked asterism names and 57 (7.5%) under the broad marking; they use 12 or 16 of 25 asterism labels, Puṣya supplies 19, and their normalised entropy (0.775, 0.835) is below that of matched non-asterism name elements (median 0.993), which are open (Chao1 2,282). Two independent markings agree with kappa 0.97. Discovery half of seed 2026-10-21-birth-star-names (666 seal legends): the direction note's N1 and N3 fail as written (prefix-plus-run compounds have 60 types and Chao1 186; no modifier distinguishes three bases); N2 is retired because the calibrated birth-star class itself is less even than matched open vocabulary. Fish runs without their stroke prefix have 33 types and Chao1 38.6, match the broad Brahmi profile at 57 occurrences, keep their four commonest forms at 62-75% across Mohenjo-daro, Harappa, Lothal and Dholavira, and are independent of the following sign (p = 0.36); runs of other sign families are as closed, and 35.6% of legends carry a fish run against 5.5-7.5% asterism names among Brahmi donors. question: Do the fish compounds on Indus seals form the closed, nearly evenly used class of about 27-28 names that birth-asterism naming would produce, measured against the asterism names of a known naming system in Lüders's 1912 list of Brahmi inscriptions?
remedy: Hashed the protocol and marking rule before extraction; used two independent markers and a logged resolution; kept every marker-A version; froze through the shared loader with nine artifacts and a single joint credence rule in which a closure failure kills the claim and a pass weighs little; replaced an upward bootstrap that rejected the claim's own model with a matched-size comparison and kept the superseded power run; wrote scoring instructions and a scorer that refuses objects already in the pinned corpus and waits for 40 fresh fish runs.

challenge: DEDR is the only primary witness and its online edition is all rights reserved, so codings stay local. Many tips are missing in many entries. The ML estimate for 'star' sits near the uninformative value because the fitted rate is high, and on the MCC tree, which splits South I first, a meaning attested only in South I can exceed 0.5 at the root. The northern star words begin with b-, which answers Tamil v- in the coded entries, and DEDR cross-refers entry 4876 to viṇ 'sky'.
outcome: Sixteen needed senses of nine words were coded from the Dravidian Etymological Dictionary on the 20 tips of the Kolipakam 2018 MCC tree (root 4,433 years). 'Star' lies in entry 4876 (miṉ 'to shine'), separate from 4885 (mīn 'fish'), and is attested in Tamil, Malayalam, Kannada, Kota, Toda, Gondi, Kurukh and Malto. Its Mk1 maximum-likelihood root probability is 0.524 and North Dravidian node probability 0.681; parsimony places it absent at the root. The needed meanings reach the root in 7 of 14 comparable cases against a reference mean of 0.54 (p = 1/10001). P1, P2 and P3 pass; the kill condition fails; the frozen rule gives credence 0.35. Posterior trees give 0.520 (89% above 0.5); a star form homophonous with mīn gives 0.41 at the root and 0.22 at the North node; DravLex fieldwork forms give 0.001. DEDR records no banyan sense for vaṭam, no squirrel sense for piḷḷai and no Murukan sense for vēḷ. Review credence 0.20.
question: Was 'star' a meaning of Proto-Dravidian *mīn, and do the meanings Parpola's readings need reach the root of the Dravidian tree more often than unproposed meanings from the same dictionary entries?
remedy: Froze sense classes, coding rules, models and the credence rule before any entry was read; recorded two post-data location decisions in an amendment and repeated the literal procedure as a sensitivity; fixed the plain-reading recodes before computing; froze the code by hash and computed once; checked the parse against the source text independently, which found a Gondi attribution error before the freeze; reproduced every root probability with an independent implementation; reported the homophone, posterior, two-rate, doubtful-form, keyword, literal-location and fieldwork sensitivities beside the primary result.
retry_when: A correspondence count of northern b- against Tamil m- and v- across DEDR (C-0011 P5), a lexical source for North or Central Dravidian independent of DEDR (P4), an openly licensed DEDR-linked lexicon that allows tracked codings, or a dated tree with the traditional South I and South II sister grouping. A rerun of the same codings on the same tree adds nothing.
theme: Root-level meanings of the Dravidian words in Parpola's Indus readings, on the dated tree of Kolipakam and colleagues
title: Was 'star' a meaning of Proto-Dravidian *mīn, and do the meanings Parpola's readings need reach the root of the Dravidian tree more often than unproposed meanings from the same dictionary entries?

challenge: Source word divisions and training tags are stronger observations than available for IVS. Rare categories, repeated identities and giant extension components constrain generalization. Word/sign length filters select different objects.
outcome: Whole-word context/identity-only accuracy is 90.41/81.79% for Sumerian, 97.00/95.09% for Egyptian, 83.92/69.23% for Greek written-unit types and 50/50% for 50 Akkadian targets. question: Can anonymous identities, context and position predict source tags on held-out source groups, with or without supplied word boundaries?

The post-outcome sign amendment and source correction retain their original counterparts.

title: Can anonymous identities, context and position predict source tags on held-out source groups, with or without supplied word boundaries?

challenge: The one-face/one-word assumption, distinct script representations, mixed source languages, incomplete lexica and independently chosen maps limit interpretation. Sanskrit dictionary-letter windows have different units and premises.
outcome: 1522 distinct IVS faces of length 3-8 have 47 equality patterns. Repeated 200-entry spelling samples give mean compatible fractions 92.02%, 97.13%, 96.93% and 91.16% for the Sumerian, Akkadian-document, Egyptian and Greek cohorts, generally with multiple candidates. Per-face correspondences do not form a shared key. A separate observed-inventory injection bound is necessary only and selects no historical language.
question: How selective are equality-pattern word matches when several known documentary spelling inventories receive the same per-face correspondence freedom?
remedy: Preserved natural lexicon counts, size-matched draws, subset intervals, ambiguity counts and exact cardinality constraints. Raw spellings/maps remain local. The manuscript keeps hypothetical mapping rules separate from source-observed records.
retry_when: A fixed shared mapping model, dated and matched reference units, verified word boundaries or independent phonetic/semantic anchors support a new withheld test. Additional flexible dictionary fits alone do not resolve this construction.
theme: lexical compatibility, dictionary size and shared-key constraints
title: How selective are equality-pattern word matches when several known documentary spelling inventories receive the same per-face correspondence freedom?

challenge: The high set was chosen after looking from 28 signs and rests on 18 discovery and 11 confirmation seals; P1a, P1b and P4 share those seals; a layout reading (a large face leaves room for an extra final sign) predicts the same association; the coordinator's review followed Shot B's confirmation outcome; the site result reversed between halves.
outcome: Discovery half (590 seals, one per component): the closing-sign size signal sat in four rare last signs (001, 595, 679, 820; 18 seals, +0.66 residual log area against -0.02); identical legends not closer in size (p 0.31). Frozen predictions scored once on the confirmation half (620 seals, 582 components): P4 pass, the 11 seals ending in the set +0.35 against -0.01 (p 0.021); P1a pass, last-sign between-sign ratio 1.81 (p 0.0074); P1b fail, frozen lexicon r 0.117 against rearrangements (p 0.060); P1c fail, closing not above opening (p 0.32); P2 fail, identical legends 0.445 against 0.512 (p 0.10); P3 fail and reversed, closing formulae site-specific (z 2.72) and first signs not (z -0.16); auxiliary P5 pass, unicorn Bull1:W seals +0.37 (p 0.0001). Kill condition not met; C-0001 credence 0.12 to 0.21. Independent recomputation agreed on P1a, P4 and the kill decision. Post-outcome (exploratory): the P4 pass rests mainly on 820 (5 seals, +0.62); 679 did not repeat; other closers carry size on the confirmation half (ratio 1.62, p 0.027). Adversarial review: the P4 pass rests on three 820 seals (dropping M-6, M-16 or M-649 gives p 0.138, 0.071, 0.066; rank version p 0.087-0.093; without 820, p 0.40); P1a's signal lies mostly outside the set; review credence 0.13. Plate check (AI readings of CISI photographs): PP1 met, PP3 passed, all seven photographed 820 seals show the closing sign at normal size and spacing; review credence 0.15, claim narrowed to 820.
question: Do the closing signs of Indus seal legends mark a grade that the seal's size also marks, beyond seal type, site and text length, and are opening signs more local than closing signs?
remedy: Two-stage design with hashed predictions, lexicon and scoring code; split-half rehearsal and power simulation before freezing; stratified permutations keeping type, site and length; one seal per component; independent recomputation with separate code and generator; post-outcome analysis confined to a dated exploratory amendment.
retry_when: Seals outside this export (later excavation reports or a new concordance) with complete legends ending in 820, 001 or 595 and measured faces; photographs showing whether those closing signs sit inside the text band; or impressions on sealings whose legends end in these signs. Do not retest the full closing-sign lexicon or the opening-closing locality contrast on the same split.
theme: conjecture shot: seal size and closing signs as marks of grade
title: Do the closing signs of Indus seal legends mark a grade that the seal's size also marks, beyond seal type, site and text length, and are opening signs more local than closing signs?

challenge: Sign-level contrasts are diluted because every sign in a legend shares its site, size and animal; within-band rearrangement leaves little for a class map to win; the metadata field `class` encodes the field animal and was missing from the strip list; aggregate facts about withheld variables were known in advance; the period field mixes two excavation sequences; only 323 of 704 discovery seal legends consist entirely of mapped signs.
outcome: Frozen primary score S = z1 + z2 = -0.567 (P1 site-concentration contrast z1 = -1.20, P2 size contrast z2 = +0.63), 33.0th percentile of 10,000 within-band rearrangements (pass threshold 2.073, the 95th percentile), 0.44 SD below their mean: fail, kill condition met, C-0002 dead. Numerals-fixed sensitivity: -0.30 SD. Individual predictions all failed: P3 unicorn z = -1.32 (p 0.898), P4 Harappa vs Mohenjo-daro tablet vocabulary z = +1.38 (p 0.082), P5 period z = -0.51 (p 0.690). Secondary checks failed: S1 commodities on steatite p = 0.051 (predicted direction), S2 740-400 vs 740-090 seal size reversed (p 0.999), S3 Spearman rho = -0.19 (n 29). Independent recomputation: S = -0.525, 34.1st percentile, fail; T2 identical, T1 within 0.00035. Exploratory: names are the most evenly spread vocabulary; determinatives, titles and the numeral form 013 are the most site-concentrated. Adversarial review: the same code gives +0.88 SD on the discovery half with real withheld fields (fail, no kill); per-sign site concentration is not reproducible between halves (r = -0.092); planted size effects of 1.2x area fail and 1.5x pass; the evidence supports 'this map fails this test', not a refutation of the grammar or glosses.
question: Does a working reading that assigns the 118 commonest signs to seven classes (numerals, links, great households, personal-name elements, commodities and units, offices, closing determinatives) with English glosses, built on the discovery half from position, neighbours, pictures and object type only, predict where confirmation-half seals were found and how large they are better than rearrangements of its own labels within frequency and position bands?
remedy: Discovery/confirmation split with sealed loader; `class` stripped; effect sizes instead of z statistics; synthetic dry runs with planted effects to state power (planted S at 3.13 SD); coordinator review reduced the primary score to P1 and P2 before freezing; hashes of predictions, map and script frozen; single logged confirmation read; independent recomputation without the scoring code; post-outcome analysis confined to a dated exploratory amendment.
retry_when: A new class map or gloss source is proposed with its own discovery-stage construction; or the reversed-locality hypothesis (shared name stock, city-specific closing vocabulary) is frozen as a protocol and tested on texts none of these analyses has seen, such as a new concordance or newly published seals (the discovery half's sites were explored by Shot A); or seal and sealing deposits supply issuer-level evidence; do not rerun this map on the confirmation half.
theme: meaning map: class and gloss map of 118 Indus signs tested on withheld object variables
title: Does a working reading that assigns the 118 commonest signs to seven classes (numerals, links, great households, personal-name elements, commodities and units, offices, closing determinatives) with English glosses, built on the discovery half from position, neighbours, pictures and object type only, predict where confirmation-half seals were found and how large they are better than rearrangements of its own labels within frequency and position bands?

challenge: Earlier packages recorded acquisitions in different schemas, so a heuristic harvest linked only 62 of 3,127 distinct source titles to a local PDF path. Some data/raw directories were unreadable to the walker. Thickness values printed as ranges and a site-name spelling variant were not anticipated by the protocol's rules. The web-check agent sent the owner's email address in a User-Agent header on four Wikimedia requests before correcting itself.
outcome: The local corpus holds 4,695 provisional objects and 5,680 faces from 78 site labels, with 8,722 CISI image crops. Object-level coverage: site 99.4%, CISI number 86.8%, excavation string 89.6%, material 82.5%, any spatial unit 76.3%, any dimension 76.6%, all three dimensions 28.8%, depth 50.6%, chronology label 55.8%, any local image 53.4%, museum value 5.8%, calendar date 0%. Faces of one object never disagree on object fields; 5,206 of 5,434 paired millimetre values equal inch values times 25.4. CISI 1 and CISI 2 are held as complete scans, so the C-0004 plate check needs no acquisition. Web checks (61 agent entries, 3 direct) found a public CC BY 4.0 transcription of the Mackay 1938 and Marshall 1931 seal tables (709 and 560 rows), CC0 or CC BY museum routes at the Met, Cleveland and Penn, public scans of several excavation reports, no open CISI edition, ICIT closed to anonymous access and no new corpus for 2024-2026. data/MANIFEST.json lists 85 sources (33 held, 9 partly held, 9 project outputs, 34 not held); tools/fetch_data.py lists, fetches and verifies them; 30 question cards Q-1001 to Q-1030 rank the work.

Added one recorded site alias for the cross-export comparison. Development outputs are preserved under data/raw/2026-10-12-data-inventory/.

outcome: 28 West Asian objects: mean u 0.770 (0.660-0.866), excess 2.11 bits per transition, p at the 1/20,000 floor; round seals 0.870 (0.776-0.945). South Asian regions 0.49-0.57; all four regional differences exclude zero. South Asian round seals 0.704 (0.531-0.872); foreign-minus-South-Asian round 0.165 (-0.026 to 0.357). Central Asian square seals 0.403. Common signs in unusual orders: 3 of 22 foreign texts end with W740 against 34.9% of comparators.
question: Do Indus-script texts found in Mesopotamia, the Gulf, Iran and Central Asia follow South Asian sign-sequence statistics, and is any deviation larger than regional variation inside South Asia?

challenge: The first run treated unlabelled copper tablets as a rival class. Two runs used 2,000 permutations where 10,000 were specified, and Haldane odds ratios were misleading.
outcome: Repeated texts stay with one image class in all three genres (p = 0.0001). Held-out image prediction succeeds on bas-relief tablets (24.8% against a 21.5% majority) and incised tablets (57.4% against 48.1%) and fails on copper (19.2% against 26.9%). The frozen within-genre conclusion therefore applies to the Harappa tablets only. Copper class-specific sign groups occur on matching-animal seals 3 times against 3.01 expected (p = 0.62); the test had power 0.91 for a fivefold enrichment and 0.22 for a twofold one.
question: Do texts on copper, bas-relief and incised tablets pair with their images, share vocabulary within an image class, and recur on seals with the matching field animal?
remedy: Corrections in runs v2 and v3 with amendments. Parpola (1994; 2008) is cited for the copper tie.
retry_when: Seals and sealings from one excavated deposit, or recoded images for the unlabelled copper tablets, permit a within-context comparison.
theme: copper and moulded tablet image-text pairing and transfer to seals
title: Do texts on copper, bas-relief and incised tablets pair with their images, share vocabulary within an image class, and recur on seals with the matching field animal?

challenge: Substitution marks distributional relatedness, which numerals or title sets also produce; the Mayig classes are one annotator's grouping; conjunct test had no power.
outcome: Variant pairs: 0.199 minimal pairs per pair against 0.018 (p 0.0005); out-of-Mayig-class variants still 4.6 times the null. Homophone base pairs: 0.083 against 0.053 (p 0.13) and neighbour divergence 0.668 against 0.677 (p 0.21). Adjacent Wells codes in different key roots, mostly stroke numerals, show the same excess as out-of-class variants. Jar-stroke ordering holds in 94 of 97 eligible texts. Table has 88 bases, 412 variants and 214 ligatures; 18 pooled values.
question: Do the key's variant groups and same-value (homophone) groups substitute in identical frames and share neighbours more than frequency-matched sign pairs?
remedy: Stratified relabelling null preserving pair structure, cluster bootstrap, Holm correction, independent verification (43/43 checks).
retry_when: A second sign list's groupings or a data-driven clustering supplies a comparison set; local-context conjunct tests are designed.
theme: sign-list structure asserted by a published key
title: Do the key's variant groups and same-value (homophone) groups substitute in identical frames and share neighbours more than frequency-matched sign pairs?

challenge: Synthetic corpora are homophonic consonant encodings of running text; real inscriptions may be formulaic, logographic or nonlinguistic. Three runs per cell.
outcome: True homophonic keys exceed their within-stratum rearrangements by 27.4, 33.2, 37.1 and 72.5 standard deviations; the published key on the real corpus by 1.2-2.4. Annealing under the correct model recovered 37-83% of tokens in seven runs and 7% in one. Language identification by half-split transfer depends on seeds: Stage 5 identified Old Tamil and Sumerian but not Sanskrit or Latin; the near-duplicate rerun identified Latin and Old Tamil, tied Sanskrit with Latin and missed Sumerian. No wrong-language model exceeded z 3.1 on novel half-B texts, while the real corpus transfers at 6.3-7.0 under all four models. Indus half B reuses 37.4% of half-A trigrams against 8.2-10.1% for synthetic corpora.
question: On synthetic corpora with the Indus shape (1,859 texts, Indus lengths, Indus sign frequencies) encoding held-out Sanskrit, Latin, Old Tamil or Sumerian, how far does the true key stand above its permutations, how much does blind annealing recover, and does half-split transfer identify the language?
remedy: Same procedure, strata and step counts as Stage 3g; held-out text not used in model training; designed after outcomes and labelled exploratory (Amendment 3).
retry_when: A formulaic or logographic synthetic generator, or segmented Indus units, change the alternative under test.
theme: identifiability of phonetic keys at Indus corpus scale
title: On synthetic corpora with the Indus shape (1,859 texts, Indus lengths, Indus sign frequencies) encoding held-out Sanskrit, Latin, Old Tamil or Sumerian, how far does the true key stand above its permutations, how much does blind annealing recover, and does half-split transfer identify the language?

challenge: Pooling both line orders biased the control. Interior lines were counted twice, boustrophedon faces were misread, and segmenter agreement was omitted.
outcome: Complete lines recur elsewhere more often than windows crossing the division: 23 faces against 4, with 42 ties, under the conservative line order (p = 0.0003). Results survive shifted-division, deduplication and numeral-line controls in review. The Dirichlet-process segmenter places a boundary at 76 of 76 divisions against 37% of other positions. Indus alternation (0.029) lies inside every matched comparison range and is descriptive.
question: Do catalogued line divisions fall at recurring-unit boundaries, and do segmented Indus units show Kober-style stem alternation beyond readable comparison corpora?
remedy: Conservative order added in v2; v3 counts lines once and excludes boustrophedon faces; segmenter agreement computed in review.
retry_when: More boundary evidence from multi-line tablets or photograph-measured spacing permits supervised segmentation.
theme: catalogued line divisions, unsupervised segmentation and alternation
title: Do catalogued line divisions fall at recurring-unit boundaries, and do segmented Indus units show Kober-style stem alternation beyond readable comparison corpora?

challenge: The Ur III value dropped units and truncated compound numbers. The item direction was assumed.
outcome: With the next sign as item, IVS has fewer values per item than Ur III at the same size (3.61 against 4.53-5.15), a larger dominant share (0.606 against 0.407-0.450) and a higher value-item information ratio (0.457 against 0.298-0.336). Post-outcome, the contrast survives unit-aware, rarefied and net-information comparisons. The preceding sign is more informative about the value. Near-fixed combinations depend on direction: 520 after three tall strokes and 585 after seven when following, and openers 861, 817 and 820 before two strokes when preceding.
question: Do Indus stroke numerals behave like Ur III administrative counts or like fixed numbers bound to particular signs?
remedy: The value construction and both directions are reported, and the genre difference is stated.
retry_when: Site- and period-stratified numeral contexts, photographic checks of the twelve-stroke grid or a larger Linear B or proto-cuneiform sample are available.
theme: counting versus fixed numeral combinations
title: Do Indus stroke numerals behave like Ur III administrative counts or like fixed numbers bound to particular signs?

challenge: The readability criterion is an emulation with Monier-Williams and DCS lexicons and a small ending set; the preprint's practice adds further freedom (inserted consonants, sandhi, other dictionaries), which would only raise the acceptance rate.
outcome: With two-consonant stems, random consonant strings at Sanskrit letter frequencies are readable from attested DCS lemmas in 91.8-96.4% of cases at lengths 4-16 and from Monier-Williams headwords in 98.5-99.7%; with one-consonant stems every non-empty skeleton is readable. The key reads 94.8% (DCS) of 1,859 unique texts, above all 1,000 within-stratum permutations (mean 88.9%, max 94.1%), but within-stratum hill-climbing reaches 99.4-99.6%; Monier-Williams: key 96.0%, permutations 93.9%, fitted 99.5%. Held-out redundancy is 0.573 for full text and 0.167 for the fifteen-class skeleton; the preprint's formula gives at most 1,980 consonants (about 790-1,760 under corrections) against 473 in the 50 longest texts. 69.2% of 1,747 published readings match the key's skeleton; most departures add unwritten consonants.
question: Does Yajnadevam's Sanskrit key read the Indus corpus more readily than rearrangements of its own values, and does his unicity-distance argument hold for the representation the key fixes?
remedy: Exact reproduction of the app's key and inherent-vowel rule, independent verification of skeletons and readability shares, local-only raw sources.
retry_when: A proposed key specifies an acceptance criterion with measured redundancy, or a new lexicon-free criterion is defined; repeating dictionary-readability tests without random-string calibration does not inform.
theme: published decipherment claims, acceptance criteria and unicity distance
title: Does Yajnadevam's Sanskrit key read the Indus corpus more readily than rearrangements of its own values, and does his unicity-distance argument hold for the representation the key fixes?

challenge: Inscriptions may be formulaic names or titles rather than running speech; the model is built from Vedic and classical text. Annealed optima partly exploit the model, so they bound achievable fit rather than estimate a true key.
outcome: Order gain under an order-5 DCS model: key -0.393, 1.2 sd above 1,000 within-stratum rearrangements of its own values (89.5th percentile); 2.0-2.4 sd under unsandhied-only training or anusvara->m; an order-only statistic places it inside its rearrangements in all settings (z -0.55 to +0.60). Held-out Sanskrit spans +0.29 to +0.42; i.i.d. strings -0.435; published readings -0.442. Within-stratum optima with unchanged consonant counts reach +0.19 to +0.23; fits to scrambled texts +0.02 to +0.04 (real order -0.22 to -0.33). Unconstrained optima (+0.47 to +0.69) delete 22-46% of signs as vowels. Under matched freedom, half-split transfer z is 7.7 Sanskrit, 8.6 Latin, 8.1 Old Tamil, 6.4 Sumerian, and 6.3-7.0 on half-B texts without near-duplicates. Stage 3e failed through a rare-class artefact and is preserved.
question: Are the key's consonant sequences Sanskrit-like under an independent model, compared with permutations of its values, optimized keys, scrambled corpora and other languages under matched freedom?
remedy: References from held-out spans, single words and random headwords; exhaustive-choice sensitivity; token-frequency-constrained repair (Amendment 2); independent verification; adversarial review.
retry_when: A new key, a model of seal-formula language, or independently segmented texts allow a held-out comparison; the same key needs no rerun.
theme: published decipherment claims, language-model likelihood and achievable fit
title: Are the key's consonant sequences Sanskrit-like under an independent model, compared with permutations of its values, optimized keys, scrambled corpora and other languages under matched freedom?

challenge: The first loader read Egyptian transliterations instead of glyph units, and the Linear B sample was too small to include.
outcome: Mean boundary F1 is 0.531 (Dirichlet process), 0.461 (greedy n-gram) and 0.431 (branching entropy), against 0.485 for a boundary everywhere. On Ur III seal legends, branching entropy reaches 0.692 against 0.557. Gold-word alternation is 0.056-0.069 in all four cohorts and does not separate them. On predicted segments it falls to 16-48% of the gold rate.
question: At the size and length distribution of the Indus corpus, do unsupervised segmenters recover word boundaries and inflectional alternation in Sumerian, Egyptian and Akkadian records?
remedy: The loader was corrected before the run, and the Linear B omission is stated.
retry_when: A segmenter is trained with boundary evidence or the corpus grows substantially.
theme: method calibration on readable scripts at Indus scale
title: At the size and length distribution of the Indus corpus, do unsupervised segmenters recover word boundaries and inflectional alternation in Sumerian, Egyptian and Akkadian records?

challenge: Uncommitted edits from earlier sessions in shared files; parallel contributors writing cards and data files; 112 free-text statuses needing judged classes; the legacy verifier rejects the newly authorised data/MANIFEST.json and reports 25 older missing targets.
outcome: AGENTS.md rewritten as a single entry point with every earlier rule and the data-first rule; README rewritten for people with dated sections moved verbatim to knowledge/TIMELINE.md (all 62 old links retained); registry split into 165 per-entry files with status_class and area, regenerated registry.json field-equal to the original; 33 finding cards, 38 general question cards, generated knowledge/MAP.md, tools/kb.py (search, show, list, next, new, build, check), seven skills, four issue forms and llms.txt. kb.py check passes with 0 errors; a second build changes nothing. Performed by Codex CLI (GPT-6.1-Sol, xhigh) from a written prompt; reviewed by the coordinator.
question: Can the repository be restructured so that many people and agents contribute in parallel from one entry point, without moving or losing any existing evidence?
remedy: Owned-path list and no-move rule in the prompt; baseline hashes of 18,871 files; per-entry preservation check; hand classification recorded in STATUS-MAPPING.md; verification outputs kept in the package.
retry_when: The contributor model changes (for example a licence or CI decision), or kb.py check reports drift.
theme: open-collaboration restructure: entry point, cards, registry split, CLI, skills
title: Can the repository be restructured so that many people and agents contribute in parallel from one entry point, without moving or losing any existing evidence?

challenge: Small regional samples; witnesses are mostly published drawings and 1932 halftones; Reader 1 was not blind to codes; British Museum images unavailable; Lipi's direction field and sign order conflict with the impressions for three Gulf seals; the inventory result admits several explanations (another language, imitation, transcription convention).
outcome: 31 Lipi records joined with evidence (15 by identifier or citation), including 25 of Laursen's 27 Indus-inscribed Gulf Type seals; CISI numbers exist only for the Indus Valley seals (C-32, M-415, M-416, M-417, M-1369, M-1370). Of 137 checked circular-seal sign positions, 2 differ from Lipi; two Gulf seals are coded in mirror order and Lipi codes pseudo-script strokes as numerals. Other round seals predict a held-out round seal 1.28 bits per transition better than matched South Asian text (interval 0.82-1.76, p = 0.001), of which 1.22 bits come from sign frequencies; shared transitions +2.8 points (p = 0.27) against +24.8 for the copper-tablet control. West Asian and South Asian circular seals do not predict each other after Holm correction. Twins-initial: 4 of 22 West Asian texts against 2 of 2,122 South Asian texts, both readers agreeing on all 28 items (Fisher p = 1.2e-7); 2 of 19 without pseudo-inscriptions (p = 0.00044).
question: Can the Lipi records of round seals be joined to Laursen's 2010 Gulf Type catalogue and to CISI, do their transcriptions agree with published images, do round-seal texts form a shared sequence tradition, and does the twins-initial pattern of West Asian texts hold with image-checked identifications?
remedy: Frozen protocol with hashes, dated amendment before computation, blinded second reader, structure-matched South Asian models and nulls, positive controls, five sensitivities including re-oriented and checked transcriptions, and an independent verifier (14 of 14 checks).
retry_when: Photographs of the Bahrain, Failaka and British Museum Ur seals, Gulf seals found since 2010, or a simulation that separates imitation from names written with chosen signs become available.
theme: Gulf Type and other round seals: catalogue joins, image-checked transcriptions, shared sequence tradition and twins-initial count
title: Can the Lipi records of round seals be joined to Laursen's 2010 Gulf Type catalogue and to CISI, do their transcriptions agree with published images, do round-seal texts form a shared sequence tradition, and does the twins-initial pattern of West Asian texts hold with image-checked identifications?

challenge: Mohenjo-daro supplies 917 of 1,430 seals; the site breakdown is post hoc with small counts; motif codes come from catalogues and M-895 is a fragment; common names would also spread across cities.
outcome: 1,430 complete single-line seals from named South Asian sites; 65 texts recur on 174 seals, 41 at more than one site. Frozen test: same-site share of duplicate pairs 0.473 against 0.448 (p 0.31, ratio 1.06). Length-stratified null: 0.473 against 0.382 (p 0.032). Post-review breakdown: Mohenjo-daro duplicates at chance (59 against 60.2 same-site pairs), Harappa 10 against 6.0, other sites 7 against 1.5 (p 0.002); about 15% of shared texts wholly local, compatible up to 25%. Identical pairs of four or more signs exceed a bigram model 3.1- to 5.3-fold; none among 445 seals of six or more signs. Motif concordance comes from unicorn pairs (88 of 89 matches); 1 of 42 pairs with another animal matches. Of 16 sealings matching seals (6 texts), 13 (4 texts) match only seals elsewhere, including Lothal L-161 to L-170 with the four-sign text of Mohenjo-daro fragment M-895.
question: Do identical Indus seal texts behave like personal names (duplicates local to one city) or like labels used across cities, and what do whole-text reuse, motif concordance and sealing-seal matches add?
remedy: Frozen protocol; exact hypergeometric and enumeration checks; length-stratified and variant-merged sensitivities; adversarial review with recomputed checks (Amendment 3).
retry_when: Plate-checked motifs and texts for L-161 and M-895, dated contexts for duplicate seals, or an object-level seal corpus of a known script allow a calibrated comparison.
theme: seal text identity, locality of duplicates and sealing matches
title: Do identical Indus seal texts behave like personal names (duplicates local to one city) or like labels used across cities, and what do whole-text reuse, motif concordance and sealing-seal matches add?

challenge: A cached reimplementation first disagreed with the frozen search because its normalization is not idempotent, and the first annealer was too slow on a shared machine.
outcome: The 362 searched and 274 multi-context codes are identical in every rearrangement. Nonempty full intersections are 164 against 158.0 +/- 10.5 (p = 0.28; annealed 255); repeated exact residuals 201 against 208.0 +/- 13.0 (p = 0.74; annealed 264). Moving the 17 new anchors to frequency-matched codes gives 395 +/- 175 windows against 256. Each code's best residual keeps its published support under rearrangement; the post-outcome residuals sam, sa and ati lose support when the anchor values move.
question: Do the October 9 Bonta-extension lexical statistics depend on which Wells codes carry which Sanskrit seed values, and do the new anchor codes open more windows than frequency-matched codes?
remedy: Exact agreement with the frozen lexical_search on four assignments, per-window caches and incremental counters checked against fresh searches, and separate null, anneal and summary stages.
retry_when: A lexical criterion with measured redundancy, such as held-out likelihood under the claimed language, replaces dictionary completion, or seed values come from evidence independent of the corpus windows.
theme: permutation and achievable-fit calibration of Sanskrit lexical windows
title: Do the October 9 Bonta-extension lexical statistics depend on which Wells codes carry which Sanskrit seed values, and do the new anchor codes open more windows than frequency-matched codes?

challenge: Role statistics depend only on the code-to-role mapping. W740 supplies 519 of the 827 excess tokens and makes the null bimodal. A transfer-step error and timing tests preceded the final runs; an independent review found an uninitialized count in the family-count annealer and a verification check of the wrong file.
outcome: 21 of 53 families meet the two-split rule against 19.9 +/- 2.9 for rearrangements (p = 0.42); optimized swaps reach 47. The code-level count is 62 against 49.1 +/- 4.4 (p = 0.003; exact maximum 115). Total excess, 827 against 194 +/- 295 (p = 0.026), is inside rearrangements once W740 is set aside (p = 0.115). No family meets the frozen per-family rule (BH q <= 0.01; smallest q = 0.026); a post-review 10,000-draw extension gives q = 0.005 for carrier/yoke and bound stalks. Fits to half the texts transfer at z = 4.5 to 4.9 against 1.9 to 2.3 for the published map. The October 11 leading codes rank first to seventh of 27 by final z in a stratum where seven codes exceed z = 3.
question: Do the anchor-expansion family roles and the October 11 positional meanings score better than within-stratum rearrangements of the same assignments, how far does the same freedom reach, and do fitted role constraints transfer between halves of the corpus?
remedy: Exact linear-assignment bounds and annealing, a labelled post-outcome stratum and W740 decomposition, a rerun from fixed seeds, recomputation with the anchor-expansion aggregate() function, and Amendment 1 with a corrected annealer (bound unchanged at 47), a resolution extension and verification-v2.json.
retry_when: A meaning map is tested against observations outside sign order, such as image-text pairing or object function, or a new family map and its roles are frozen before positional results are seen.
theme: permutation and achievable-fit calibration of family role coherence and positional sign meanings
title: Do the anchor-expansion family roles and the October 11 positional meanings score better than within-stratum rearrangements of the same assignments, how far does the same freedom reach, and do fitted role constraints transfer between halves of the corpus?

challenge: The coders worked from code-ordered sheets with counts. The adoption code ranked the finer family partition first. Steps 2-5 ran before this endpoint.
outcome: Two codings by instances of one model agree (ARI 0.884 unweighted, 0.975 token-weighted). Base families gain 0.0219 and 0.0222 bits per sign (0.0190 and 0.0193 net of the 0.0029-bit identity partition), above all 200 random partitions (p = 0.005). Unseen-sign loss falls from 14.60 to 14.19 bits; P and M groupings reach 13.93 and 13.94. Post-outcome: contiguous cuts of the Wells order gain 0.0164 on average and none reaches 0.0219. Modifier signatures fail (p = 0.11), and none of nine modifiers passes alone.
question: Do graphic base families, published sign-list groupings and modifier classes predict the contexts of the original Wells codes better than random groupings of the same sizes?
remedy: Disclosed in the report. The amendment adopts coder 2's coarser partition and records the run order.
retry_when: A human coder recodes from shuffled sheets without counts, or photograph-based coding of the low-agreement families is available.
theme: componential sign coding and grouping prediction test
title: Do graphic base families, published sign-list groupings and modifier classes predict the contexts of the original Wells codes better than random groupings of the same sizes?

challenge: Segment statistics became unreliable after the rehearsal. The numeral-order calibration failed on Ur III because of the value definition, and the typology table is unverified.
outcome: Indus initial-sign entropy exceeds final-sign entropy: asymmetry +0.260 against a shuffle range of -0.017 to 0.018, and +0.149 without the 35.2% of texts ending in 740. In comparison corpora the statistic changes sign with unit and genre: Ur III seal legends score -0.204 by sign and +0.079 by word. It is therefore descriptive, and every candidate language remains tied under the frozen rule.
question: Does a structural profile of Indus texts separate candidate language families when compared with readable seal and record corpora?
remedy: A pre-computation amendment substituted whole-text statistics. The calibration cause is reported, and the typology status is stated.
retry_when: At least two head-initial and two head-final seal-legend corpora are measured at sign and word level with the same code.
theme: whole-text structural profile and language-family typology
title: Does a structural profile of Indus texts separate candidate language families when compared with readable seal and record corpora?

challenge: A concurrent allograph study overlapped step 1. Steps 2-5 ran before step 1's endpoint. Review found overstated conclusions, a missing protocol output and several small code faults.
outcome: Diagnosis saved as a direction memo with an interactive map of 158 paths. Six steps ran under a protocol recorded before outcomes. Graphic families improve prediction of rare signs, mostly through information already in the Wells order. Harappa tablet texts pair with their images within genre, with no detectable transfer from copper to seals. Catalogued line divisions fall between recurring units. Stroke values are more tied to neighbouring signs than Ur III counts are. Unsupervised segmentation and alternation fail to discriminate at Indus scale. Indus texts close on a small sign class, a descriptive property. Every ledger description failed at least one frozen prediction, and every candidate language remains tied.
question: Which analytical mistakes have kept the project from a substantive result, and what do sign-list, image-text, segmentation, numeral, rehearsal and structural tests on material already held establish?
remedy: Step 1 was scoped to a different question. Seventeen review findings were accepted, with dated amendments, new endpoints for steps 2 and 3, rewritten reports and recorded responses. Earlier runs are preserved.
retry_when: A head-final seal-legend corpus, photograph-measured sign spacing, a within-deposit seal and sealing frame or a shuffled-order human sign coding becomes available; reuse the frozen code on the new population.
theme: diagnosis of the research program and a six-step structure-before-meaning plan
title: Which analytical mistakes have kept the project from a substantive result, and what do sign-list, image-text, segmentation, numeral, rehearsal and structural tests on material already held establish?

challenge: Harappa and copied face modules dominate; one graph component has 222 of 312 prototypes. Declared side counts disagree for five primary objects. The selected prototype-bag law differs from original-copy-bag permutation then deduplication. Broad administrative field labels are observationally equivalent.
integration_status: Prepared standalone entry; global registry not edited by administrative contributor.
outcome: 417 all-recorded-clean RTL objects yield 312 matched prototypes and 17 tall-stroke/W700 anchor classes with variable levels. Copied bundle collisions are 423 versus 141.192 under full-module allocation (Holm p=.001). The W034/W700 depletion expresses face-role occupancy: 103 faces contain both codes; preserving W700 slot roles reduces expected cross-face exposure from 23.485 to .957 and leaves no adjusted sign-pair maximum below .05. Copying persists (423 versus 190.940, Holm p=.002). A standing-capacity-token life cycle and identity, issuer, package, commodity and canonical receipt rivals have explicit independent physical predictions. Four synthetic graphic distributions are exactly equivalent under their latent field interpretations.
question: Do whole face modules bind beyond site/type/length margins and copying, and what carrier operations could the observed architecture implement?
remedy: Freeze intact-module allocation before outcomes, keep all faces and aliases before filters, use full-search maxima and 10-test Holm adjustment, preserve original endpoint, add dated post-outcome W700-role control, retain independent exact counterexample, and specify carrier histories and controlled physical observations.
retry_when: New independently registered carrier histories, physical attachment/cancellation/use traces or stamped vessel capacities can distinguish predeclared operational variants. Additional transcriptions, broad metadata or relabelled graphic fields do not resolve current role equivalence.
theme: multiface administrative records and operational identification
title: Do whole face modules bind beyond site/type/length margins and copying, and what carrier operations could the observed architecture implement?

challenge: Final-only grouping hid carrier closing blocks; substitution summaries omitted two codes; literal joins missed attested compounds. Site enumeration and normalization required correction. Public class images hide exact font variants. Initial CLI auth failed before later user subscription login.
outcome: Seven leading candidate families cover nine codes; W158 rejoins the qualified carrier complex and W617 remains a lower segmentation lead. The viewer has 713 codes, 56 selected Sanskrit senses and 20 bounded examples. Claude Opus 5.5 subscription review completed and its hand counts were checked. Fixed analytic maxT uses 1,388 active comparisons; W142 medial p is 0.461108. Joined lexical rival ranks and crosswalk sensitivities are published.
question: Which proposed new meanings retain useful evidence after literal lexical rivals, position multiplicity, variant and source-image checks?
remedy: Preserve earlier endpoints; add fixed-moment diagnostics, formula/length/substitution/segmentation audit and finite-join rival tests. Verify vivadha, matya and kaṅkata anchors, correct sense fields and disclose protocol deviations. Complete external and separate Codex reviews; build run-v6.

theme: conditional semantic extension and adversarial review
title: Which proposed new meanings retain useful evidence after literal lexical rivals, position multiplicity, variant and source-image checks?

challenge: Literary complexity alone cannot date a convention or identify its source. Practical success can validate several variants rather than the model's exact reference. A root sentence overstated the memory graph's node types, and one literal reviewer probe rejected correct wording. Concurrent research was editing the shared workspace.
outcome: Integrated two studies in a manuscript and 11-claim evidence map. A separate RV10.95/Śatapatha11.5.1 control separates wording, later framing and instructions. An exact synthetic retention model preserves all 180 scenarios; its primary twenty-step procedure and attribution probabilities are 0.9891304 and 0.5057646 under invented laws. Independent source, package and mathematical capsules pass 3,212 current checks with no unresolved substantive blocker. The working historical thesis remains unconfirmed at the level of a diagnostic Harappan-to-textual join.
question: Can selective inheritance and intellectual recombination explain mature early textual knowledge while preserving distinct historical tests for particular Harappan contributions?
remedy: Kept archaeological, compositional, redactional, manuscript and narrated time distinct; attributed disputed scholarly assessments; froze the synthetic law before calculation. Repaired prose scope and the literal checker while preserving attempts and endpoints. Saved 13 selected starting-byte snapshots, a broad start inventory and current navigation bytes before integration. Source payloads stay local-only.
retry_when: A new independently dated carrier, unusual linked operation bundle, parallel-recension comparison or recovery-controlled assemblage can discriminate the predeclared routes. Preserve this package and write the empirical continuation to a new dated directory.
theme: mature early Indian knowledge, source control and adversarial synthesis
title: Can selective inheritance and intellectual recombination explain mature early textual knowledge while preserving distinct historical tests for particular Harappan contributions?

challenge: Crop occurrence, scaled assemblage percentages, divine role lists, finished beads and legendary policy accounts represent different observations. The first filter did not require a retained linked text after removing textual observations. The preliminary Sanauli comparison does not establish local manufacturing.
outcome: Fourteen works or editions supply 30 observations and seven claims. Developed a selective-survival mechanism through households, apprenticeships, patrons and specialist teaching. Rice uncertainty reassignment preserves one narrow Masudpur VII direction but broader ranges overlap and no quantified PGW domestication endpoint is available. Corrected eligibility gives five initial hypotheses, two source-reported intermediate archaeological candidates and zero diagnostic cross-domain joins. DN16 supplies an observed conceptual transfer of meeting principles across institutions.
question: Which practices and organizational relations could survive settlement reorganization and contribute to mature early Indian textual institutions?
remedy: Retained source loci, competing routes, strata and uncertainty; preserved audit.py/run-v1, documented an amendment and wrote audit-v2/run-v2 separately. Independent review reproduced filters and visually checked rice Tables 2-4. Four prospective tests specify production, recovery and textual controls.
retry_when: Independently dated intermediate production contexts, recovery-controlled farming evidence or assessed role-action loci distinguish unusual linked practices from imports, convergence, inherited Indo-Iranian repertoires or later institutional construction. Additional generic similarities alone do not identify a route.
theme: practical and institutional transmission beyond decipherment
title: Which practices and organizational relations could survive settlement reorganization and contribute to mature early Indian textual institutions?

challenge: Narrated time, composition, witnesses and physical river processes can be confused. Parallel digital editions share ancestry. A wrong chapter, an English transcription glitch and a publication-year mismatch required source control. A synthetic erasure construction can be mistaken for empirical redaction or complexity generation.
outcome: Eighteen source records and 17 observations qualify Manu/Iḍā ritual relations, Rigvedic rivers and DN27's storage-property-authority sequence, with Iranian and transmission controls. The typed graph blocks ten unsupported date transfers and accepts two own-text presence controls. A declared rewrite maps 10,368 invented histories to one account after annotation erasure; retaining route, time, actors or all annotations gives 4, 108, 24 or 10,368 outputs. Developed practical retention and changing-origin mechanisms, plus an explicitly post-audit narrative-reset hypothesis. No diagnostic Harappan memory chain was identified.
question: Which parts of sophisticated early Indian origin accounts could preserve older practical relations, and which observations could identify their historical route?
remedy: Preserved failed/corrected acquisitions; checked exact Sanskrit/Pali loci; kept river reaches and access scope separate; corrected Allon to 2022 and confined the manuscript control to its Gāndhārī discourse variant. Independent enumeration and graph reproduction confirm the stated constructions. Prospective tests compare branches, recoverable procedure signatures, specific river configurations and reset accounts.
retry_when: Independent textual branches or material assemblages test a predeclared rare relation bundle and intermediate carrier. Compare operational and attribution changes with shared ancestry and genre controls; use independent identity and composition constraints for any river-event test.
theme: cultural memory, operational relations and origin narratives
title: Which parts of sophisticated early Indian origin accounts could preserve older practical relations, and which observations could identify their historical route?

challenge: A mixed comparison retained full Lipi sequences and an access record contained a signed download URL. Nested Windows paths caused false file/link omissions; a concurrent working README edit affected the first anonymous-content comparison.
outcome: Filtered exactly two local-only source/access paths from the two published branch histories. The final screen checked 14,465 blobs, with zero known credential/signed-URL matches, forbidden paths or oversized blobs. A pristine checkout passed 983 Markdown documents, 50 catalogue manifest hashes and 362 drawing paths. GitHub public visibility and anonymous commit/README access were verified.
question: Can the research repository be made public while preserving frozen local evidence and excluding unresolved-rights payloads and access artifacts?
remedy: Keep original local bytes, private all-ref bundles and selected-working-tree backup. Filter only exact paths in an isolated mirror, correct Windows path handling without editing frozen evidence, verify a pristine checkout, use an atomic two-branch push with explicit leases, and check anonymous access against the immutable publication commit.
retry_when: Any newly acquired or copied source material needs its own asset review; no automatic public upload of raw corpora.
theme: repository preservation and public asset review
title: Can the research repository be made public while preserving frozen local evidence and excluding unresolved-rights payloads and access artifacts?

challenge: Several reports share excavation lineages; structural phases cannot resolve annual work windows. Well estimates, finished products, inferred apprenticeships and crop diversity differ from measured output or independent capacity. Preliminary Dholavira access failed and a modern interpretive wrapper was unsuitable.
outcome: Fourteen inspected works supply 34 observations. Harappa Mound E records a clogged drain followed by a new culvert route. Dholavira Stage VI follows desertion and combines selected reservoir-support walls with salvage and changed settlement layout; one named eastern reservoir separately lost its water function and hosted later activity. Craft and provisioning sources motivate support-chain and shared-input tests. All 34 coded observations leave the six demand, delivery and work quantities unresolved, so no numerical Harappan minimum is estimated.
question: Which Harappan observations distinguish the continuation of a place, service and production capability, and which quantities would establish a renewal requirement?
remedy: Preserved acquisitions and exclusions, obtained the original archived preliminary report and inspected the reservoir pages. Distinguished direct observations, author interpretations and post-audit hypotheses. Prospective tests retain occupation breaks, alternative inputs, recovery controls, residents' access and independent quantity bounds.
retry_when: New delivered quantities, wear/output estimates, independent import ceilings, local co-use chronology, measured operation durations or skill/participation evidence permit a source-qualified bound or schedule comparison. Do not convert broad phase duration or provider counts into an annual maintenance budget.
theme: Observed maintenance, rerouting, selective retention and support chains
title: Which Harappan observations distinguish the continuation of a place, service and production capability, and which quantities would establish a renewal requirement?

challenge: Counts and phase units differ; selected mound validation cannot identify regional recall. Aliases, historical-map filters, unreachable target horizons, landform chronology and context association constrain inference. Source supplements and historical inventory lineage remain unresolved. Initial P18 bounds, one area attribution, merged demotion rules and profile-level pilot wording needed correction. CLI authentication/path handling and DOI/diagram print layout required repairs.
outcome: A 12,362-word reviewed manuscript and 33-page PDF use 69 cited references from 72 source records, 50 local witnesses and 21 editorial regions. Historical 96/roughly 1,000 counts cannot form a current fraction with 142 Early and Mature excavations through 2024. Ganweriwala estimates of 81.5, 66.7 and approximately 33 ha have different spatial definitions. Local comparisons distinguish confirmed recording omissions, missing map associations, remote proposals and finer mound units. A source/effort concordance precedes a proposed 24-block preservation pilot; no national site or artifact total is fitted.
question: Why do recorded and excavated Indus-site counts differ, what can area estimates and repeat surveys establish, and which overlooked settings warrant discriminating investigation?
remedy: Preserved five draft/revision endpoints and three numerical runs; inspected primary count, chronology and anchor observations; used shared-frame cells, block-level inference and adequacy denominators; separated archaeological survival from Indus attribution and operational feasibility. Two actual Claude Opus 5.5 reviews with tools disabled and commissioned Codex passes precede the final text. Successor registers resolve audit clarifications. Final source/output/export verification passes 41 checks, with 50 witnesses ignored and 69 complete PDF reference targets.
retry_when: Accessible reconciled project-level records and exact surveyed footprints, new local dates or preservation/detection calibration permit a new discriminating result. A named partner and verified access are required for field tasks. Do not repeat national artifact extrapolation, naive capture-recapture or site-size inference from geographic proximity using the same aggregate evidence.
theme: Excavation coverage, hidden settlement landscapes and archaeological survey design
title: Why do recorded and excavated Indus-site counts differ, what can area estimates and repeat surveys establish, and which overlooked settings warrant discriminating investigation?

challenge: An unrestricted minimum list can misidentify political institutions or assume local closure. Separate cost sums can double-count shared operations. Preserving current work and source scope matters in a shared research workspace.
outcome: A manuscript, conditional theory and 15-claim evidence map join independent delivered-output bounds, actual renewal operations, joint work windows and historically available enactment. Shared repair and learning develops a concrete alternative to separately costly training. The framework explains why urban form, residents and practical knowledge can have different persistence outcomes; a particular Harappan-to-textual contribution remains a separate historical test.
question: What minimum functional conditions does a complex society need over a stated horizon, and how can longevity and renewal traces make those conditions archaeologically testable?
remedy: Define outcome, boundary, horizon and distribution before necessity claims; include carried inventory, substitution, imports, co-production and action information. Commission independent mathematical, source and manuscript review. Preserve 12 selected starting-byte snapshots and a 16,316-file start inventory, append navigation over current bytes, and retain earlier endpoints and local-only source witnesses.
retry_when: A predeclared service sequence or common sampling frame supplies independent demand/supply bounds, dated replacement operations and participation evidence. Extend with a new dated empirical study and include short-lived, interrupted and uncertain cases.
theme: Conditional minimum functions, renewal inference and practical knowledge
title: What minimum functional conditions does a complex society need over a stated horizon, and how can longevity and renewal traces make those conditions archaeologically testable?

challenge: Purposive coverage cannot estimate field-wide omission or establish general novelty. Acquired articles and selected reading differ; book access, publisher challenge pages, edition identity and shared witnesses limit scope.
outcome: The literature frame records 28 sources, including 25 primary works read at declared scopes, 45 observations and seven prospective comparison records. Direct predecessors cover simultaneous reproduction, viable futures, repair and learning, joint scheduling, polycentric organization and coupled institutional pathways. Inspected duration/network studies do not supply the demand, initial-output, import and renewal inputs needed by the proposed archaeological inference procedure.
question: What existing theories and recommendations address the continuing provision of complex societies, and what archaeological measurements would develop them?
remedy: Preserved actual reading depth, query history, source loci, edition corrections, failed routes and local-only witnesses. Source integrity passes 312 checks and branch packaging passes 129; neither reanalyzes the published studies.
retry_when: A new close predecessor changes the bounded assessment, or a systematic sample of a defined literature tests the prevalence of a specific measurement. Do not repeat a broad priority claim from this purposive frame.
theme: Economic reproduction, maintenance, viability and archaeological persistence
title: What existing theories and recommendations address the continuing provision of complex societies, and what archaeological measurements would develop them?

challenge: Results depend on action costs, skill eligibility, shock severity, observation timing and the specified horizon. Technical selection does not establish distributed implementation, fairness, historical frequency or archaeological parameters.
outcome: A frozen 36-state model enumerates 32 worlds, finite horizons and infinite sets. Budget 1 with aging skill permits three primary safe transitions without shocks, whereas nonaging skill permits indefinite survival. Budget 2 exceeds mean work 4/3 but cannot sustain state (1,1,1) indefinitely under separate costs. A post-baseline shared repair/training law enumerates 16 worlds and removes selected deficits: budget 1/no-shock and budget 2/all original supports become indefinitely viable from the primary state. challenge: Graphic prediction, generated correspondence recovery, fitted quantities and historical interpretation have different input requirements; short source-defined records were largely absent from the main predictor's population.
outcome: Reviewed the 101-entry baseline and four papers. All 66 Harappa tablet faces and 353 of 355 nominated numerical-class rows fall outside the principal length filter. question: Which existing observations and tools can support a restricted Indus reading, and what independent evidence is missing?

retry_when: A named independent quantity, referent, original source packet, corrected specimen join or historically justified reference changes the readiness of a specific test. Use the named prior audit before repeating a capability experiment.

challenge: Creation dates are missing for repeated marked groups; accession collisions, incomplete mass and mixed marks limit comparisons. Catalogue line breaks and grouping errors affected census v1. The Gonur original inventory and newer Susa chapter remain unavailable.
outcome: Joined Susa SB13677/AS2615 to its museum record and reconstructed the published 25:1:2 weight proposal, requiring 0.944619% symmetric variation. Censused 69 explicitly coded Susa entries, with 57 eligible mass/mark ratios. Audited all 938 Greater Indus weight entries including 870 Dholavira objects. Located the Gonur 26-token hoard's original figure and context recovery targets.
question: Can western and Central Asian sources join repeated marks to masses, counts, units or complete inventories?
remedy: Retain attributed historical coefficients, calculate exact sensitivity intervals, preserve census v1 and correct it in v2, exclude unresolved collisions, audit complete catalogue coverage and name exact registrations, rooms and plate targets.
retry_when: Dated marked-weight assemblages, all-face mark photographs, a readable unit control, Gonur Fig.41 and inventory, or DHR context joins supply new source observations.
theme: western and Oxus numerical bridges
title: Can western and Central Asian sources join repeated marks to masses, counts, units or complete inventories?

challenge: Inventory, mass, material and mark descriptions disagree. One imported weight has distant creation and deposition periods. The Ascalone 2023 route returned login HTML.
outcome: Recovered three signed mass discrepancies, including AS 13820 changing from 2769 g to 3067 g. Two original ducks described as unmarked conflict with modern stroke counts. question: Do original catalogues and museum images support the modern marked-weight packets?
remedy: Preserve source-specific descriptions and measurements, reject HTML as a PDF, retain provisional accession joins, separate creation and deposition, and preserve the earlier fit. No new fit was run.
retry_when: Independent SB/AS concordance, conservation/weighing history, all-face marked photographs, dated assemblages or AS13855 modern registration resolves a source disagreement.
theme: Susa mass, mark and context source audit

challenge: The Tondur impression is dark; the modern 408 object identity and a common depth unit are missing. The compound image route returned 403 XML and the 2018 route returned 500 HTML. An extracted name and chapter end needed correction.
outcome: The original 2005 report joins a proposed 408 reading to AGM-2, depth 1.40 m, stratum 2 and drawing 2. The original Tondur account joins three reported horizontal strokes to three beds in Panchanampadi cave. question: Can source numeral readings be joined to physical referents or registered contexts?

retry_when: A readable Tondur impression plus bed census, original 408 accession, exact graffiti/Tamili concordance, calibrated vessel capacity or independently documented specimen quantity becomes available.

challenge: The API supplies separate context margins without joint specimen quantities or dates. Apparent full-book downloads were a brochure and a preview. Complete component naming excluded useful compounds in the initial calculation.
